tagline.text: Palawan's "prison without walls," where inmates farm their way through their sentences

location.label: Location
location.text: Along South Road in Barangay Iwahig, south of Puerto Princesa

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day (about 1–2 hours of visiting)

children.text: Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm is an open prison set up by the American colonial government in 1904, where inmates live and work in rice paddies and fields. South of Puerto Princesa, it is a frequent city-tour stop, and you can buy handicraft souvenirs made by inmates.

Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm lies in Barangay Iwahig, south of Puerto Princesa on Palawan Island, and is one of the seven operating units of the Philippine Bureau of Corrections. It is said to hold about 4,000 inmates today. The word "farm" is in the name because inmates serve their sentences not behind high walls but on wide farmland, doing rice and vegetable farming, fishing, forestry and carpentry. For that reason Puerto Princesa tourism sources also describe it as a "prison without bars." Because it looks so different from the prisons most people imagine, it has become a distinctive city-tour stop for travelers.

The history goes back to the Spanish era. Under Spanish rule, Puerto Princesa was a place of exile for banished convicts, and because malaria was endemic it was regarded as practically a death sentence. The present prison farm began on November 16, 1904, during the American occupation, when Governor-General Luke Wright authorized a penal colony on Palawan. It started at about 22 acres (about 9 ha) to take prisoners that Bilibid Prison in Manila could not accommodate, and its first superintendent was Lt. George Wolfe. William Cameron Forbes modeled the design on the George Junior Republic, an American self-governing youth community. Inmates were divided into three classes, and the top two classes, with good conduct and diligence, were given about 2 ha of land to cultivate themselves. That old system is why, even now, you may see the families of some inmates living nearby.

The World War II story is also worth knowing. During the Japanese occupation, the superintendent Pedro Paje led about 1,700 inmates and 45 staff and guards while secretly supplying food and medicine to the Palawan underground resistance and keeping watch over the American prisoners of war held in Puerto Princesa. President Manuel Quezon allowed inmates to be used for sabotage and intelligence work, and Paje posed as a Japanese collaborator as cover. This overlaps in time with the Palawan Massacre of December 1944 at nearby Plaza Cuartel. Keeping in mind that Iwahig is both a tourist stop and a historic site makes a visit more meaningful.

This guide is for travelers who can spare about half a day from Puerto Princesa to see Iwahig. The way visits work, opening hours and entry procedures can change over time. Blogs and information pages give slightly different opening hours, and because this is a correctional facility, visits can be restricted without notice, so it is best to check the latest situation with a local tour operator or your accommodation before you set out. Take special care with photography, clothing and how you treat the inmates. Rather than treating it only as a sight, please visit with a respectful attitude and a wish to understand this unusual institution.

The first surprise at Iwahig is that you hardly see high walls or barbed wire. Low buildings, rice fields and modest houses are scattered across wide land, and you can see inmates tending rice and vegetables or doing fishing and carpentry work. Inmates serving long terms for serious crimes, however, are kept in a separate secured area.
Along the road and in the shop at the information center, bags, wallets, wood carvings and key chains made by inmates are sold. Prices are said to start from
, so they are easy on the budget, and the money is said to go to the inmates' livelihood and welfare. Bring plenty of cash.
About
2.5km

inside from the entrance checkpoint are the community center and the information center, which have an exhibit on the facility's history and a souvenir shop. Visitors report that the inmates working in the shop often speak English, so short conversations are possible.

According to traveler reports, a low-risk inmate sometimes acts as the guide. The color of an inmate's clothing indicates their level of freedom, and brown is said to mean the inmates with the most freedom. How guiding works can differ from visit to visit, so follow the instructions on site.

Lonely Planet and others note that when tour groups visit, inmates perform dance routines in the gymnasium of the central compound. Not every independent traveler will see one, so check whether your timing matches a group tour.

Around the central area, administrative buildings, a recreation hall and a community center are scattered among the fields. The road lined with green paddies and palm trees feels very different from the roads in the city, and walking it is an unusual experience even if you take no photos.

blocks.title: Superintendent Pedro Paje and the guerrilla story

children.text: The story of how the superintendent secretly helped the Palawan underground resistance during World War II is a hidden highlight of Iwahig. Ask a guide, or read it alongside exhibits at Palawan's museums, to understand it better.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: From the city to Iwahig and back

children.text: Take a tricycle or taxi from your hotel in Puerto Princesa and set out for Iwahig. The ride from the city is said to take about
30~40 minutes
At the entrance checkpoint, leave your ID and receive a numbered tag. The trunk of your vehicle may also be checked.
Go in as far as the information center and the community center, see the history exhibit and browse the handicrafts in the shop.
Quietly look around the farmland and the inmates at work in the permitted areas. Always ask permission before taking photos.
On the way out, return the tag and collect your ID, then head back to the city for lunch.
Opening hours are said to be around
in various guides, so arriving in the late morning is the safe choice. If you arrive early in the morning it may not be open yet, so check.

items.title: City tour combination
items.subtitle: Plaza Cuartel, the cathedral and Iwahig

children.text: Walk around Plaza Cuartel and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in the city center.
Go to Iwahig Prison and see the information center and the souvenir shop.
Return to the city for lunch, then continue to the Palawan Museum or other city-tour sights.
Most Puerto Princesa city tours include Iwahig as a midway stop. Tours usually take half a day to a full day, and prices and inclusions differ by operator, so check before you book.
Flights run from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), and the flight takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
or so.
Flights and fares vary a lot by season, so check the airline's app a few weeks before departure.

items.title: From the airport or city to Iwahig

children.text: According to the Puerto Princesa city tourism guide, Iwahig is about
30 minutes
from both the city and the airport, and a tricycle with up to three people costs about
. Another guide also lists about ₱400 one way.
A 2014 blog says a multicab (small shared vehicle) to Iwahig costs ₱50, but another guide says there is no regular shared transport. Check locally whether a shared ride is available.
The distance from the city is described differently by different guides, at about
. It is safest to arrange your ride back to the city in advance.
If you charter a vehicle, a waiting charge for the round trip may be added. Agree on the price and waiting time with the driver before you leave.
If you include it in a Puerto Princesa city tour (cathedral, Plaza Cuartel, museum, Iwahig and so on), you do not have to worry about transport separately.
You can also charter a van through your accommodation or a travel agency.
Iwahig involves a lot of walking outdoors, so the dry season is more comfortable. In Puerto Princesa the dry season is roughly December to May.
Because opening hours are limited to the daytime, plan so you do not arrive too late in the day. To avoid the heat, right after opening or the late afternoon is best.

There is no accommodation at Iwahig itself, so you stay in Puerto Princesa and make the trip from there. Rizal Avenue in the city center and the area around the Baywalk have many hotels and restaurants, which makes it easy to combine a city tour or an underground river tour in your schedule. If you stay in the city, you can visit Iwahig in the morning and still return to the city for lunch.

Food options inside Iwahig have not been confirmed, so eat in the city before you go or bring a few snacks and water. In the city you can easily find Palawan seafood restaurants and Filipino local eateries, and returning around noon after a morning visit works well.
At the entrance checkpoint you leave your ID and receive a numbered tag. Be sure to bring your passport or an ID.
The trunk of your vehicle may be inspected, so leave unnecessary items behind.
Dress in light but neat clothing. Clothes that cover your shoulders and knees are the safe choice.
Treat inmates and staff politely, and always ask permission before taking photos.
Do not enter administrative areas or residential areas marked with signs prohibiting entry.
Pay for souvenirs in cash. Do not show large bills, and bring plenty of small change.
Arrange your transport back from the city in advance. Public transport is scarce, so a car that waits for you round trip is convenient.
Opening hours and visiting rules change often, so check the latest notices before you leave.
This is a real correctional facility where inmates live, so it is a place for quiet and courtesy, not a sight to gawk at. Breaking the rules may get your visit restricted.
Do not photograph the faces of inmates and staff without permission.
Do not hand money or goods directly to inmates. Buy properly at the shop.
Do not enter areas with prohibition signs, and follow the guide's instructions.
Visiting hours and permitted areas can change without notice, so follow local guidance.
If you cannot secure a ride back, you may be stuck until late, so prepare in advance.
The central city of Palawan, north of Iwahig, has a cathedral, Plaza Cuartel, museums and restaurant streets. It takes about
30 minutes
to travel from the city.
Known as a UNESCO World Heritage site, the underground river is the signature Palawan activity. Getting there takes long, so it is usually booked separately from Iwahig rather than on the same day.
An island-hopping area in the sea north of Puerto Princesa. It lies in a different direction from Iwahig, so it is better scheduled for a different day.
Famous as an archaeological site, it is far to the south, so it is better visited as a separate trip.
